historical_name_rule: Real historical names, places and dates allowed. No living private identities.

source_cards.title: A call to stay off buses
source_cards.maker: Women’s Political Council members and local leaders
source_cards.purpose: To get people to join a protest
source_cards.body: Jo Ann Robinson and other organisers helped spread a leaflet. It asked Black residents to avoid the buses on Monday 5 December. The first call was for one day. The protest then grew into a much longer boycott.
source_cards.question: Does a call to act prove that everyone joined?
source_cards.help: It is useful for what organisers asked people to do. It cannot count how many joined.
source_cards.staff: The King Institute catalogue marks the leaflet’s author and 2 December date as uncertain. Its note identifies WPC preparation and later editing by a committee of local leaders. Early December is used on the pupil card; do not attribute every version to one author. The extended boycott is context from H1, not a statement that the first leaflet planned a year.

source_cards.title: The early demands
source_cards.maker: MIA leaders, Martin Luther King Jr and U. J. Fields
source_cards.purpose: To ask the bus company to change its rules
source_cards.body: The MIA was the group that led the boycott. Its early demands included polite treatment, seats taken in order of arrival, and Black drivers on mainly Black routes. The seating plan still placed Black riders from the back and White riders from the front. These demands did not yet seek fully mixed seating.
source_cards.question: Does a list of demands prove they were met?
source_cards.help: It gives evidence of leaders’ aims at that time. It does not prove the company agreed.
source_cards.staff: MIA means Montgomery Improvement Association. The document catalogue gives an approximate 8 December date; the historical overview reports formal demands on 8 December. First-come seating was proposed within a front/rear arrangement, not a demand to retain reserved empty seats. Do not turn early limited demands into full integration from the outset.

source_cards.title: Keeping the protest going
source_cards.date: A later history, updated in 2022, about 1955–1956
source_cards.purpose: To explain how the boycott worked
source_cards.body: Many people walked or shared car rides so they could stay off buses. Volunteers drove and helped arrange lifts. The MIA raised money to support this work. The campaign needed many people and steady effort, not just one famous leader.
source_cards.question: Can a short history tell us about every journey?
source_cards.help: It helps explain how people travelled during the boycott. The broad account is checked against another history. It leaves out many daily details.
source_cards.staff: The NPS and King Institute accounts agree on carpools, volunteers and fundraising. They differ on some counts and the MIA founding date; those disputed details are not used. Later histories can combine records but must be checked, including institutional sources. Do not claim that every boycotter used the carpool.

source_cards.title: The court ruling
source_cards.kind: Court decisions described in a later history
source_cards.maker: Courts made the rulings; the King Institute wrote the later history
source_cards.purpose: To explain court decisions about bus segregation
source_cards.body: Four Black women challenged bus segregation in the case Browder v. Gayle. On 5 June, federal judges ruled against the segregation laws. On 13 November, the US Supreme Court upheld that ruling. The legal case mattered as well as the boycott.
source_cards.question: Does a court ruling tell us how every rider was treated?
source_cards.help: The account gives evidence of a change in law. A legal ruling cannot show every person’s daily experience.
source_cards.staff: This card summarises the King Institute’s account of the decisions, cross-checked with NPS; the original court opinion is not supplied. The district court majority was two to one. Four plaintiffs continued the case after a fifth original plaintiff withdrew. Rosa Parks was not a plaintiff in Browder v. Gayle. Name women and lawyers if helpful without suggesting that one leader secured the change alone.

source_cards.title: A call to end the boycott
source_cards.maker: Martin Luther King Jr for the MIA
source_cards.purpose: To announce the next step after the court order arrived
source_cards.body: The court order had reached Montgomery. King announced that the boycott was ending. He asked Black residents to return to buses the next morning with the seating rule removed. His call shows what the leaders wanted people to do next. It does not, by itself, show every bus journey.
source_cards.question: How could we check whether the plan happened?
source_cards.help: It is strong evidence of the public announcement. Check another account for what happened the next day.
source_cards.staff: The historical statement is paraphrased without any quotation. The King Institute’s editorial note and overview record integrated buses on 21 December 1956. This is a check beyond the statement’s call. Ending segregation on buses did not remove every discriminatory rule or end racism. No slurs, testimony or violence details are needed.

context: In Montgomery, Alabama, USA, racist bus rules kept Black and White riders apart. Black residents had challenged these rules for years. model: S1 tells me that organisers asked people to avoid buses on 5 December. The lesson writer made this card. A campaign group made the leaflet behind it to gain support. I trust it for the plan. It does not prove that every person took part. I would check an account of what happened.

hinge.question: S1 called on people to avoid buses. Which claim can it best support? A: Organisers wanted people to join. B: Every person joined. C: All unfair rules ended.
hinge.answer_and_decision_rule: A. The leaflet gives evidence of a call to act. It cannot prove total take-up or the result. If a pupil chooses B or C, model plan versus result, then use the parallel check before independent work.
hinge.parallel: S2 lists demands. Does it prove the bus company agreed? No. It shows what leaders asked for; we need later evidence to check the result.

staff_care_rules: Teach racism factually and calmly. No copied slurs, discriminatory seating, victim simulation, role play or personal disclosure. Do not ask pupils to defend racist rules or imagine being a targeted person. Historical names and dates are allowed; no living private identities or local school details are used.

Agree the quiet signal, usual supervising adult, safe place and return check before starting. Keep all pupils supervised. If the sole adult cannot safely supervise separate spaces, pause the group or offer a calm area in the room while using the normal support route.

Acknowledge distress without probing. Stop the demand and offer the agreed pause without sanction or a public explanation. Follow existing safeguarding arrangements for disclosures. Do not require a catch-up discussion while a pupil is upset.

Stop racist or flippant remarks calmly and firmly, name the harm without repeating a slur, correct the fact and reset respectful language. Check those affected and follow up privately. Use school procedures for repeated, targeted or serious incidents; do not stage a debate about whether racism is valid.

Enquiry: What helped the campaign change bus rights?
In Montgomery, Alabama, USA, racist bus rules kept Black and White riders apart. Black residents had challenged these rules for years. Rosa Parks was arrested on 1 December 1955 after refusing to give up her seat. The bus boycott began on 5 December. Many people worked together to seek change.
Date
Event
5 December 1955
The boycott starts. People stop using buses as a protest.
5 June 1956
Federal judges rule against bus segregation in Browder v. Gayle.
13 November 1956
The US Supreme Court upholds the ruling.
20 December 1956
The court order arrives. The MIA ends the boycott.
21 December 1956
People return to buses with the old seating rule removed.
Use sources with care
People’s protest, shared rides, funds and a legal case all mattered. One person did not do it alone. Bus rights changed; racism did not end.
A leaflet shows a call to act. A court decision shows a legal ruling. A short history can bring facts together. None can tell us everything.
MIA means Montgomery Improvement Association. It helped lead the boycott.

Judge reasons, not a memorised trust label. Every card is a new lesson-writer summary, dated 2026. The maker of the evidence behind it must also be named. No original record, image, testimony or quotation is supplied.
S1 A call to stay off buses
Maker and purpose: Women’s Political Council members and local leaders; to get people to join a protest.
Use and limit: It is useful for what organisers asked people to do. It cannot count how many joined.
The King Institute catalogue marks the leaflet’s author and 2 December date as uncertain. Its note identifies WPC preparation and later editing by a committee of local leaders. Early December is used on the pupil card; do not attribute every version to one author. The extended boycott is context from H1, not a statement that the first leaflet planned a year.
S2 The early demands
Maker and purpose: MIA leaders, Martin Luther King Jr and U. J. Fields; to ask the bus company to change its rules.
Use and limit: It gives evidence of leaders’ aims at that time. It does not prove the company agreed.
MIA means Montgomery Improvement Association. The document catalogue gives an approximate 8 December date; the historical overview reports formal demands on 8 December. First-come seating was proposed within a front/rear arrangement, not a demand to retain reserved empty seats. Do not turn early limited demands into full integration from the outset.
S3 Keeping the protest going
Maker and purpose: US National Park Service; to explain how the boycott worked.
Use and limit: It helps explain how people travelled during the boycott. The broad account is checked against another history. It leaves out many daily details.
The NPS and King Institute accounts agree on carpools, volunteers and fundraising. They differ on some counts and the MIA founding date; those disputed details are not used. Later histories can combine records but must be checked, including institutional sources. Do not claim that every boycotter used the carpool.
Court evidence and the campaign result
Friday 15 January 2027 | P2 | 40 minutes | Year A
Humanities | GROW | Spring 1 Week 2 | HUM-GROW-S1-W02
S4 The court ruling
Maker and purpose: Courts made the rulings; the King Institute wrote the later history; to explain court decisions about bus segregation.
Use and limit: The account gives evidence of a change in law. A legal ruling cannot show every person’s daily experience.
This card summarises the King Institute’s account of the decisions, cross-checked with NPS; the original court opinion is not supplied. The district court majority was two to one. Four plaintiffs continued the case after a fifth original plaintiff withdrew. Rosa Parks was not a plaintiff in Browder v. Gayle. Name women and lawyers if helpful without suggesting that one leader secured the change alone.
S5 A call to end the boycott
Maker and purpose: Martin Luther King Jr for the MIA; to announce the next step after the court order arrived.
Use and limit: It is strong evidence of the public announcement. Check another account for what happened the next day.
The historical statement is paraphrased without any quotation. The King Institute’s editorial note and overview record integrated buses on 21 December 1956. This is a check beyond the statement’s call. Ending segregation on buses did not remove every discriminatory rule or end racism. No slurs, testimony or violence details are needed.
An illustrative conclusion
Teacher-written model, attributed to no real person. The campaign challenged unfair bus treatment. S3 shows how shared rides helped people keep the boycott going. S4 shows that the legal case overturned bus segregation laws. Together, the sources suggest that organised protest and legal action both helped change bus rights. They cannot tell us how every rider was treated.
A source can be useful and limited
A campaign leaflet has an aim to persuade. That makes it useful evidence of the organisers’ message, not automatically false. A court ruling is authoritative about the legal decision, but cannot prove equal treatment in every encounter. A later account can compare records; age or institutional status does not make it automatically complete.
S1, S2, S4 and S5 are accessed through the King Institute. Agreement among these cards is not four fully independent confirmations. S3 also uses NPS for the shared-ride account; known inconsistent details are excluded rather than silently treated as settled.

S2 lists demands. Does it prove the bus company agreed? No. It shows what leaders asked for; we need later evidence to check the result.

A purpose to persuade means false: instead ask what claim the source can support. Official means complete: separate a legal decision from daily life. Old means true: check maker, purpose and other evidence. Summary equals original: name both layers and acknowledge what cannot be inspected.
